blocks.text: Davidson defines pneumonia as an **acute respiratory illness** with **newly appeared shadowing on chest imaging**, which may be segmental, lobar or multilobar. Kumar describes it as **inflammation of the lung substance**, usually bacterial and occasionally viral or fungal, typically presenting with acute cough, purulent sputum, breathlessness and fever plus clinical or radiological **consolidation**.
A practical bedside definition: **compatible symptoms** (fever, cough, purulent sputum, dyspnoea) **plus a new infiltrate** on chest imaging. No new shadow, no pneumonia.

blocks.title: Classification by setting (setting predicts the organism)
rows: New pneumonia **≥ 2 days (48 h) after admission**
Early onset (within 4–5 days): CAP-like. Late onset: Gram-negatives, Staph. aureus incl. MRSA, anaerobes
HAP in a **mechanically ventilated** ICU patient (≥ 48 h after intubation)
≥ 2 days in hospital in the past **90 days**, haemodialysis, IV antibiotics, or nursing/long-term care residence
Usual organisms **plus opportunists**: Pneumocystis, fungi, mycobacteria, Nocardia, P. aeruginosa

blocks.title: Other terms you must be able to define
items: **Lobar pneumonia**: uniform consolidation of one or more whole lobes, often with pleural inflammation.
**Bronchopneumonia**: patchy alveolar consolidation centred on inflamed bronchi and bronchioles, frequently in **both lower lobes**.

**Atypical pneumonia**: caused by organisms that do not grow on routine culture and are not seen on Gram stain; they **do not respond to penicillins** but do respond to macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
**Aspiration pneumonitis**: chemical lung injury from inhaled gastric contents **without infection**; secondary bacterial infection may follow within 24–72 h.
**Lung abscess**: localised suppuration with a **cavity** on CXR or CT, often with a **fluid level** (always an air–liquid interface).
**Empyema**: pus in the pleural space.

blocks.text: **HAP definition differs between books.** Davidson: a new pneumonia at least **2 days after admission**, with HCAP (healthcare contact in the last **90 days**) kept as a separate category. Kumar and K&C Essentials stretch HAP to include anyone in a healthcare setting (including nursing homes) in the last **3 months**. Use Davidson’s wording in the exam.

**Streptococcus pneumoniae** is the single commonest cause of CAP (35–80% of UK cases in K&C Essentials). Spread is mostly by **droplets**. In 30–50% of cases no organism is ever identified, and about 20% are **mixed infections** (Kumar). US data in Pocket Medicine find no pathogen in 50–60% and a virus alone in about a quarter.

blocks.title: CAP organisms (Davidson)
items: **Bacteria**: Strep. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staph. aureus, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Klebsiella pneumoniae.
**Viruses**: influenza and parainfluenza, measles, herpes simplex, varicella, adenovirus, CMV, **coronaviruses** (SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV).

blocks.title: Clinical clue → likely organism
rows: Young adult; headache and malaise for days before chest symptoms; few chest signs
Older patient with COPD or other chronic lung disease
Hotel or institutional stay, contaminated water/cooling towers/air-conditioning; hyponatraemia, lymphopenia
Recent influenza; IV drug use or central line (staphylococcal septicaemia)
Farm animals, abattoir or hide workers
Recent travel to the Middle East

blocks.title: Factors that predispose to pneumonia
items: Smoking, alcohol, recent URTI or **influenza**, old age (and Kumar adds age < 16).
**Pre-existing lung disease**: COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, an obstructing lesion.
Immune impairment: **glucocorticoids** and other immunosuppressants, **HIV**, diabetes, CKD, malnutrition.
IV drug use; indoor air pollution.

blocks.title: Hospital-acquired pneumonia: organisms and risk factors
items: **Organisms**: Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter) and **Staph. aureus including MRSA**; IV antibiotics within the last 90 days raise the risk of multidrug resistance.
**Weakened defences**: steroids, diabetes, malignancy, poor post-operative cough, bulbar or vocal cord palsy.
**Aspiration**: reduced consciousness, immobility, dysphagia (especially after **stroke**), nasogastric tubes.
**Organisms carried into the airway**: endotracheal tubes, tracheostomy, contaminated nebulisers or ventilators.
**Bacteraemia**: abdominal sepsis, infected IV cannula, septic emboli.

blocks.title: Aspiration and the immunocompromised host
items: Aspiration and suppurative pneumonia: mixed oral flora, e.g. **Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides fragilis**. An abscess in a previously **healthy lung** suggests **Staph. aureus or Klebsiella**.
Inhaled **gastric acid** (classically during anaesthesia, especially in pregnancy) causes a destructive chemical pneumonia: **Mendelson’s syndrome**.

Immunocompromised: consider Gram-negatives (especially **P. aeruginosa**), viruses, fungi, mycobacteria and **Nocardia**; infection is often polymicrobial, and pneumonia is the leading cause of death in this group.
**Pneumocystis jirovecii**: long-term steroids, methotrexate or monoclonal antibodies, transplant anti-rejection drugs, HIV with a low CD4 count.

blocks.text: Atypical organisms: “**Legions of psittaci MCQs**” = **Legion**ella, Chlamydia **psittaci**, **M**ycoplasma, **C**hlamydophila pneumoniae, **Q** fever (Coxiella).

**Legionella** is likely when **3 of 4** are present: a viral-type prodrome; dry cough, confusion or diarrhoea; **lymphopenia** without a big leucocytosis; **hyponatraemia**. The exam patient has just come back from a hotel holiday.

Where aspirated material lands depends on posture and bronchial anatomy. Davidson: **dependent segments**, e.g. the **apical segment of the lower lobe** when supine. Kumar: **right middle lobe** and the apical/posterior segments of the **right lower lobe**. K&C Essentials: the **posterior segment of the right lower lobe**.

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: Systemic upset dominates: **fever, rigors**, malaise, loss of appetite, headache, sometimes **delirium**.
Cough is at first **short, painful and dry**, later producing **mucopurulent** sputum; **rust-coloured** sputum suggests pneumococcus; occasional haemoptysis.
**Pleuritic pain**, which may be referred to the **shoulder or anterior abdominal wall**.

blocks.title: Examination
items: Start with **respiratory rate, pulse, BP and mental state**: these drive the severity judgement.
Consolidation: **dull percussion**, **bronchial breathing** (as loud in expiration as inspiration), **whispering pectoriloquy** and coarse **crackles**.
The lung passes through exudation, **red then grey hepatisation**, and resolution.
Herpes labialis points to pneumococcus.

blocks.text: Older patients often present **atypically**, with **delirium** or recurrent **falls** rather than cough or breathlessness, and may not mount a fever. Absent fever in the elderly is itself listed as a marker of severe CAP.

blocks.title: CURB-65 (Davidson, hospital): 1 point each
rows: **Confusion**: mental test score ≤ 8, or new disorientation in person, place or time

blocks.title: What the score means (Davidson)
rows: **Hospital-supervised** treatment: short-stay admission or supervised outpatient care
Manage in hospital as **severe pneumonia**; assess for **ICU**, especially at **4–5**

blocks.note: Look at: the hospital CURB-65 algorithm — five features on the left, three management boxes by score on the right.

blocks.title: Other markers of severe CAP
items: More than one lobe involved on CXR.
**PaO2 < 8 kPa** or a rising PaCO2.
Albumin **< 35 g/L**; **hyponatraemia**.
**Positive blood culture**.
Comorbidities; absence of fever in the elderly.

blocks.text: **CRB-65** drops the urea and is used in the community where a blood result is not available. Mortality rises with the score: under 5% at 1, about 15% at 3, over 25% at 4–5.

**Cut-offs differ by source.** Davidson: RR **> 30**, diastolic **< 60**, age **> 65**, confusion = mental test score **≤ 8**. Zero to Finals (NICE): RR **≥ 30**, diastolic **≤ 60**, age **≥ 65**. Kumar: confusion = AMT **< 10**. Kumar also says a score of 3+ “often needs ITU”, whereas Davidson says treat as severe and assess for ICU especially at 4–5. Follow Davidson.

Investigations aim to **confirm the diagnosis**, **grade severity** and **detect complications**. Mild CAP treated at home needs **no microbiology** and no routine CXR unless it fails to improve. Every admitted patient needs at least a **CXR, FBC, U&E and CRP**; moderate–severe cases add **sputum and blood cultures** (before antibiotics) and **urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens**. Offer an **HIV test** to everyone with pneumonia.

blocks.title: Blood tests in CAP (Davidson)
rows: WCC **> 20 or < 4 × 10⁹/L** = severity marker; neutrophils **> 15 × 10⁹/L** suggest a bacterial cause; haemolytic anaemia occasionally with Mycoplasma
Deranged if a basal pneumonia inflames the liver; **low albumin** = severity marker
When **SaO2 < 93%** or clinically severe: ventilatory failure, acidosis

blocks.title: Bloods that hint at the organism
rows: Neutrophil leucocytosis; very high inflammatory markers
WCC usually **normal**; if anaemic check **Coombs test** and **cold agglutinins** (haemolysis)
**Lymphopenia** without marked leucocytosis, **hyponatraemia**, low albumin, raised transaminases

blocks.title: Microbiology
items: **Sputum** Gram stain and culture; a good sample has < 10 squamous cells per low-power field, and bacterial pneumonia gives a purulent sample.
**Blood cultures** before antibiotics in moderate–severe CAP.
**Urinary antigens**: pneumococcal (sensitivity about 70%, specificity > 90%); Legionella antigen detects only **serogroup 1**, so a negative test does not exclude Legionella.
**Oropharyngeal PCR** for Mycoplasma and other atypicals.
**Serology**: Mycoplasma IgM, or a **four-fold rise** in titre between an early and a 10–14-day sample.

blocks.title: Chest X-ray
items: **Lobar pneumonia**: patchy opacity becoming uniform lobar consolidation, often with an **air bronchogram**.
**Bronchopneumonia**: patchy, segmental shadowing.
**Staph. aureus**: multilobar shadowing, **cavitation, pneumatoceles**, abscesses.
**Right middle lobe** pneumonia: opacity below the horizontal fissure and loss of the **right heart border**.
CXR changes can **lag behind** the clinical picture: if the first film is normal but CAP is suspected, repeat it after 2–3 days.
A CXR some weeks later (about **6 weeks**) checks for an underlying **bronchial carcinoma**.

blocks.note: Look at: sputum Gram stain — Gram-positive diplococci (Strep. pneumoniae).
Look at: right middle lobe consolidation — opacity under the horizontal fissure, lost right heart border; lateral view shows the anterior middle lobe.
Look at: left lower zone lobar pneumonia — ill-defined opacity with no volume loss (trachea and mediastinum central).

blocks.title: HAP and the immunocompromised
items: Suspect **HAP** with purulent sputum or secretions, new infiltrates, an unexplained rise in oxygen need, core temperature **> 38.3°C**, and leucocytosis or leucopenia.
Unlike CAP, **seek microbiological proof** in HAP: in ventilated patients use BAL, protected brush specimens or endotracheal aspirates.

Immunocompromised HRCT: **focal unilateral** opacity favours bacteria, mycobacteria or Nocardia; **bilateral** opacity favours Pneumocystis, fungi or viruses; a **halo sign** suggests aspergillosis; effusions point to pyogenic bacteria and are **uncommon in Pneumocystis**.
**Pneumocystis** CXR: diffuse bilateral shadowing starting **perihilar** and spreading out like a **butterfly**; confirm by immunofluorescence on **induced sputum or BAL**.

blocks.title: Differential diagnosis
items: Pulmonary infarction/embolism; pulmonary oedema (can be unilateral); pulmonary haemorrhage.
Pulmonary or pleural **tuberculosis**.
Pulmonary eosinophilia; hypersensitivity pneumonitis; cryptogenic organising pneumonia.
Malignancy, e.g. bronchial or bronchoalveolar cell carcinoma.

blocks.text: **Procalcitonin** rises in bacterial but not viral pneumonia. **CRP lags**: it can be modest on arrival and peak a day or two later even while the patient improves, whereas the WCC changes faster. Immunocompromised patients may not raise their markers at all.
Symptoms lasting **more than 2–3 weeks**, especially with **weight loss or night sweats**, should make you think of TB or fungal infection rather than ordinary CAP.

The three pillars are **oxygen, fluid balance and antibiotics**, with nutritional support in severe or prolonged illness. The first antibiotic dose should be given **promptly**: Kumar says within **1 hour** of recognising high-risk features, without waiting for results.

blocks.title: Supportive care
items: **Oxygen** to keep **PaO2 ≥ 8 kPa (60 mmHg)** or **SaO2 ≥ 92%**; high concentrations (≥ 35%) unless the patient has **hypercapnic COPD**. Consider **CPAP** in HDU/ICU if hypoxia persists.
**IV fluids** if severe, elderly or vomiting; antihypertensives may need to be paused.
**Analgesia** for pleuritic pain (paracetamol, co-codamol, NSAIDs; opiates only with great care).
**Physiotherapy** is not routine; it helps only if pain makes the patient suppress cough.
Admitted patients: **LMWH thromboprophylaxis** and **TED stockings** unless contraindicated.

blocks.title: Empirical CAP antibiotics (Davidson Box 17.40, adapted from BTS)
rows: IV **flucloxacillin** 1–2 g four times daily **plus** IV clarithromycin
**Clarithromycin** (or erythromycin), adding IV **rifampicin** in severe cases
IV **clarithromycin plus** IV co-amoxiclav **or** ceftriaxone **or** cefuroxime (alternative: IV amoxicillin plus flucloxacillin)

blocks.title: Route and duration
items: **5 days** is enough for most uncomplicated pneumonia; **Legionella, staphylococcal and Klebsiella** pneumonia need longer.
Oral treatment is adequate unless the illness is severe, consciousness is impaired, the swallow is lost, or absorption is unreliable.
Switch IV to oral once the patient has been **afebrile for 24 h**.

blocks.title: Specific organisms
rows: Macrolide (clarithromycin, erythromycin or azithromycin) for 7–10 days
Clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin or rifampicin for **14–21 days**

blocks.title: Other settings (Davidson)
rows: Antipseudomonal cover (**meropenem**, antipseudomonal cephalosporin or piperacillin–tazobactam) **plus MRSA cover** (vancomycin or linezolid). _A. baumannii_: usually carbapenem-sensitive; colistin if resistant
Start broad cover at once: 3rd-generation cephalosporin or quinolone **plus** antistaphylococcal agent, or antipseudomonal penicillin **plus** aminoglycoside

blocks.title: Refer to ITU (Davidson Box 17.39)
items: CURB-65 **4–5** and not responding quickly.
Persistent hypoxia: **PaO2 < 8 kPa** despite high-flow oxygen.
**Progressive hypercapnia** or **severe acidosis**.
**Circulatory shock**.
**Falling conscious level**.

blocks.text: **Prognosis and follow-up.** Fever can last several days and the CXR may take **weeks to months** to clear, especially in the elderly. A repeat CXR before discharge is unnecessary if recovery is good; arrange review at about **6 weeks**, with a CXR if symptoms or signs persist or malignancy is suspected. Mortality: **< 1%** in non-severe adult CAP, **5–10%** in hospital, up to **50%** in severe disease; HAP about **30%**.

**Aspiration pneumonia regimen differs.** Davidson: **amoxicillin + metronidazole**, noting that co-amoxiclav covers the same organisms but raises the risk of **C. difficile**. Kumar: co-amoxiclav for mild–moderate disease. K&C Essentials: always include metronidazole. Davidson is the exam answer.

**Course length varies.** Davidson: **5 days** for uncomplicated pneumonia. Zero to Finals: 5 days for mild, 7–10 days of dual therapy for moderate–severe. K&C Essentials: 7–10 days in total. Pocket Medicine: CAP 5–7 days, HAP/VAP 7 days, empyema/abscess 2–6 weeks.

US books use different empirical regimens: ward CAP = **ceftriaxone + azithromycin** or a respiratory fluoroquinolone; HAP/VAP = piperacillin–tazobactam, cefepime or a carbapenem **plus** vancomycin or linezolid. Also: **daptomycin is inactive in the lung**, avoid quinolones if **TB** is possible, and steroids are **not routine** in CAP (avoid in influenza).

sections.title: Complications, slow resolution and lung abscess

blocks.title: Complications of pneumonia (Davidson Box 17.41)
items: **Parapneumonic effusion** (common) and **empyema**.
**Lobar collapse** from retained sputum.
**DVT and pulmonary embolism**.
**Pneumothorax**, particularly with **Staph. aureus**.
Suppurative pneumonia and **lung abscess**; ectopic abscesses (Staph. aureus).
**ARDS**, renal failure, multi-organ failure.
Hepatitis, pericarditis, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis.
Arrhythmias such as **AF**; fever due to drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.text: **Parapneumonic effusions** complicate roughly one-third to one-half of CAP and are usually simple exudates. Suspect **empyema** when fever and inflammatory markers stay high despite the right antibiotics. Aspirate any more-than-trivial effusion under **ultrasound guidance** and send it for Gram stain, culture, protein, glucose and LDH (Light’s criteria), with **pH** as well. An empyema needs **urgent drainage**, a longer antibiotic course, and sometimes thoracic surgery.

blocks.title: Why is the pneumonia not resolving?
rows: Resistance (MRSA, Pseudomonas), wrong dose or duration, poor adherence, malabsorption
Obstructing bronchial tumour, bronchiectasis, TB, recurrent aspiration
PE, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, eosinophilic pneumonia, pulmonary haemorrhage, heart failure

blocks.title: Lung abscess and suppurative pneumonia
items: **Causes**: aspiration, Staph. aureus or Klebsiella pneumonia, inadequately treated CAP, bronchial obstruction (tumour, **foreign body**), septic emboli, TB, infarction, spread from an amoebic liver abscess.
**Risk factors** for aspiration: poor dentition, alcohol, sedation, seizures, stroke, bulbar palsy.

**Features**: large volumes of sputum, often **foul-smelling** and blood-stained (a sudden gush if the abscess ruptures into a bronchus), **high swinging fever**, pleural rub, weight loss; **clubbing** can appear within **10–14 days**.
**Imaging**: cavity with an **air–fluid level**; CT; **bronchoscopy** to exclude carcinoma or a foreign body.
**Treatment**: prolonged antibiotics (**4–6 weeks** in some); physiotherapy; surgery if no response; remove any obstructing lesion. Pulmonary actinomycosis needs **6–12 months** of penicillin.

blocks.text: Named abscess syndromes: **PVL-producing CA-MRSA** → rapidly progressive necrotising pneumonia. **Lemierre’s syndrome** (Fusobacterium necrophorum) → sore throat, then internal jugular thrombosis and septic lung abscesses. **IV drug users** → blood-borne abscesses with **tricuspid** endocarditis.
**Staph. aureus** pneumonia: patchy consolidation breaking down into abscesses seen as **cysts** on CXR; pneumothorax, effusion and empyema are common, and mortality exceeds **25%**.

blocks.title: Community-acquired pneumonia
items: **Stop smoking**: smoking is an independent risk factor for CAP.
**Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines** for those at highest risk: age **over 65**, chronic lung, heart, liver or kidney disease, diabetes, immunosuppression.
Unvaccinated older patients admitted with CAP should get the **pneumococcal vaccine before discharge** (Kumar).
**Legionella** usually has to be **notified** so the source can be traced.
In poorer settings, protect children by tackling **malnutrition and indoor air pollution** and immunising against **measles, pertussis and Hib**.

blocks.title: Pneumococcal vaccines
rows: Weak T-cell activation: short-lived antibody, **no lasting memory**
Capsular polysaccharide linked to protein, **13 serotypes** (Davidson)
Protein conjugation recruits **T-cell help** and memory (same principle as Hib vaccine)

blocks.text: US practice (Pocket Medicine): pneumococcal vaccine for everyone **> 65** and for 19–64-year-olds with heart failure, lung disease, cirrhosis, diabetes, alcohol use, smoking or immunosuppression (including asplenia and HIV), as **PCV20 alone** or **PCV15 followed by PPSV23** a year later. Inactivated influenza vaccine is advised for everyone over **6 months**.

blocks.title: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (mortality about 30%, so prevention matters)
items: **Hand hygiene** and clean equipment.
Reduce **aspiration** risk.
**Limit PPI** stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
Oral decontamination with **2% chlorhexidine**.
**Selective digestive decontamination** in some ICUs when ventilation is expected to exceed **48 h**.

blocks.title: Specific prophylaxis
items: HIV with a **low CD4 count**: oral **co-trimoxazole** against Pneumocystis.
Influenza: **droplet precautions** for inpatients; high-risk contacts can receive **oseltamivir for 7 days** or a single dose of baloxavir.

blocks.text: **SARS-CoV-2** was identified in **Wuhan in December 2019** and causes **COVID-19**. Its case fatality (about 1–5% in Kumar) is lower than SARS-CoV, but it is **far more transmissible**. Earlier coronavirus pneumonias were **SARS** (2002–03: more than 8000 cases, about 800 deaths) and **MERS** (from 2012, camel source, about **35% mortality**, with large outbreaks **inside healthcare settings**).

blocks.title: COVID-19: what to know
items: Spread **person to person** by respiratory particles, including from **asymptomatic** people; incubation up to **14 days** (median 4–5).
Of symptomatic patients about **81%** mild–moderate, **14%** severe (hypoxic), **5%** critical (ARDS, shock, multi-organ failure).
Features: fever, cough, dyspnoea, myalgia, GI upset, **loss of smell or taste**.
Severe-disease risk: age **≥ 65**, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, stroke, lung disease, CKD, **obesity**.

blocks.title: Hospital practice for a patient with pneumonia
items: Take a **travel and contact history**: unusual pathogens (e.g. MERS after the Middle East) change the plan.
Test with **RT-PCR** on a nasopharyngeal, lower-tract or anterior nasal sample; rapid antigen tests are **less sensitive**.
CXR typically shows **bilateral, peripheral** opacities but may be normal early; use **CT** if in doubt.
Isolate: the coronavirus model is an **airborne infection isolation room** with **contact plus airborne precautions** and **PPE** for staff.
Laboratory clues to **MERS-CoV** (Davidson): **lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and a raised LDH**, with rapid progression to respiratory failure and ARDS; confirm by PCR.

blocks.title: COVID-19 treatment by severity (Pocket Medicine, US NIH)
rows: Rapidly rising O2 need, ventilated or ECMO
Dexamethasone **plus** anti-IL-6 (**tocilizumab**) or a JAK inhibitor (**baricitinib**)
**Anticoagulation** (prophylactic or treatment dose) because thrombosis is common

blocks.text: **Spike-protein vaccines** are highly effective at reducing severity even when infection occurs; follow local isolation and quarantine guidance.

Steroids are **not routine** in bacterial CAP and should be **avoided in influenza**, yet **dexamethasone** is standard for hospitalised COVID-19 needing oxygen. Davidson has no COVID-specific section, so these points come from Pocket Medicine.

cards.back: An acute respiratory illness with **newly developed radiological shadowing** (segmental, lobar or multilobar).
A new pneumonia **at least 2 days after admission**; in ventilated ICU patients it is called **VAP**.

cards.front: Five atypical pneumonia organisms (“Legions of psittaci MCQs”)?
cards.back: Legionella, Chlamydia psittaci, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Q fever (Coxiella).

cards.front: Severe pneumonia after influenza with cavities/cysts on CXR and pneumothorax: organism?

cards.back: Confusion (MTS ≤ 8/new disorientation); Urea > 7 mmol/L; RR > 30/min; BP systolic < 90 or diastolic < 60; Age > 65.
0–1 home; 2 hospital-supervised; ≥ 3 severe pneumonia in hospital, assess for ICU especially at 4–5.

cards.front: How may an older patient with pneumonia present?
cards.back: Atypically: **delirium** or recurrent **falls**, often without cough, breathlessness or fever.

cards.front: When is an ABG indicated in CAP?
cards.back: When **SaO2 < 93%** or the clinical features are severe.

cards.front: Cold agglutinins are positive in what proportion of Mycoplasma pneumonia?
First-line oral antibiotic for uncomplicated CAP (Davidson)?
cards.back: **Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily**; clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic.
IV **clarithromycin plus** IV co-amoxiclav, ceftriaxone or cefuroxime.

cards.front: Davidson regimen for aspiration pneumonia, and why not co-amoxiclav?
Radiological hallmark of a lung abscess?
Serotypes in the pneumococcal polysaccharide vs conjugate vaccine (Davidson)?
Hospitalised COVID-19 patient needing oxygen: treatment?

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man had a hip fracture fixed 6 days ago. He is breathing spontaneously on the orthopaedic ward when he develops a temperature of 38.6°C, purulent sputum and a new right basal infiltrate on chest X-ray.
questions.leadIn: How is this pneumonia best classified?
questions.explanation: A new pneumonia starting **at least 2 days after admission** is **hospital-acquired** (nosocomial). At day 6 it is also **late-onset**, so Gram-negatives and Staph. aureus are more likely.
whyNot: He has been in hospital for 6 days, so the infection was acquired in hospital.
VAP needs mechanical ventilation; he is breathing on his own.
Pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury after inhaling gastric contents; nothing suggests aspiration, and he has purulent sputum.
Nothing in the history suggests immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure has a fever and cough. Her chest X-ray shows patchy, poorly defined alveolar shadowing scattered through both lower zones, centred on the small airways, with no single lobe uniformly opacified.
questions.leadIn: Which term best describes this pattern?
questions.explanation: **Bronchopneumonia** is patchy alveolar consolidation linked to bronchial and bronchiolar inflammation, often in **both lower lobes**. Lobar pneumonia is homogeneous consolidation of a whole lobe.
whyNot: Lobar pneumonia gives uniform consolidation of one or more whole lobes, not scattered patches.
An abscess is a localised cavity, often with a fluid level.
Empyema is pus in the pleural space, not alveolar shadowing.
Infarction is a differential diagnosis of pneumonia, not a name for patchy consolidation centred on inflamed small airways.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man returns from a week in a large air-conditioned hotel. He has a dry cough, diarrhoea and confusion. Sodium is 126 mmol/L and he is lymphopenic without a marked leucocytosis.
items.explanation: Hotel water systems, diarrhoea, confusion, **hyponatraemia** and **lymphopenia** point to **Legionella**. Confirm with a urinary antigen.

items.stem: A 21-year-old student had headache and malaise for 4 days before a dry cough began. The chest signs are scanty, yet the X-ray shows extensive shadowing. Target lesions appear on his palms.
items.explanation: **Mycoplasma**: young adult, a prodrome before chest symptoms, a CXR worse than the signs, and **erythema multiforme**.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man who drinks heavily is admitted very unwell with bacteraemia and dense upper-lobe consolidation.
items.explanation: **Klebsiella** is specifically linked with **alcohol misuse** and a severe bacteraemic illness.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman is recovering from influenza when she becomes severely unwell with pneumonia. Her chest X-ray shows several thin-walled cystic spaces, and she then develops sudden pleuritic pain from a pneumothorax.
items.explanation: Two steps: **post-influenza** pneumonia suggests **Staph. aureus**, and **pneumatoceles/cysts** with a **pneumothorax** confirm it.

questions.theme: Severity assessment and place of care in community-acquired pneumonia
questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
options: Treat at home with oral antibiotics
Short hospital stay or hospital-supervised outpatient care
Admit and manage as severe pneumonia
Respiratory clinic referral in 6 weeks only

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia is alert and orientated. RR 22/min, BP 124/80 mmHg, urea 5.1 mmol/L. Use the Davidson CURB-65 criteria.
items.explanation: CURB-65 = **0**, so she is likely suitable for **home treatment**.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with CAP is alert. RR 24/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, urea 9.4 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Age > 65 and urea > 7 give a score of **2**: **hospital-supervised** treatment (short stay or supervised outpatient).

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with CAP scores 7 on a mental test. RR 26/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, urea 8.3 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Confusion (MTS ≤ 8), urea > 7 and age > 65 give **3**: manage in hospital as **severe pneumonia**.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man is newly disorientated. RR 34/min, BP 86/50 mmHg, urea 12 mmol/L.
items.explanation: All five criteria are met (score **5**), so assess him for **ICU**; a score of 4–5 is the strongest trigger.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Blood tests show: WCC 3.1 × 10⁹/L, CRP 120 mg/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, ALT slightly raised, neutrophils 2.2 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Which result is a recognised marker of severity?
questions.explanation: Davidson lists a **WCC < 4 or > 20 × 10⁹/L** as a severity marker. Other markers include urea > 7, hyponatraemia, low albumin and bacteraemia.
whyNot: CRP is raised but non-specific; it is not a listed severity criterion.
This sodium is normal; **hyponatraemia** would be the severity marker.
Mildly abnormal LFTs occur when a basal pneumonia inflames the liver; it is low albumin that marks severity.
The neutrophil count matters for cause (> 15 suggests bacteria), not as a stand-alone severity criterion.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history is treated for right upper lobe pneumonia. He recovers well clinically and is ready to go home.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?
options: Clinical review with a chest X-ray at about 6 weeks
CT chest on the day of discharge
No further imaging at any stage
Daily chest X-rays until the shadowing has gone
questions.explanation: A CXR need not be repeated before discharge if recovery is good, because shadowing may take weeks to months to clear. Review at **about 6 weeks**, with a CXR when malignancy is a concern (a heavy smoker); persistent shadowing suggests an **obstructing bronchial carcinoma**.
whyNot: Not needed when recovery is satisfactory; the film will still be abnormal.
Not routine; the first step is the 6-week review and CXR.
He is a heavy smoker, so an underlying tumour must be excluded.
Radiological clearing lags behind clinical recovery; daily films add nothing.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with CURB-65 0 pneumonia had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child.
items.explanation: Uncomplicated CAP with **penicillin allergy**: oral **clarithromycin** (or erythromycin).

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with CURB-65 4 pneumonia. No drug allergies. No organism is known yet.
items.explanation: **Severe CAP**: IV clarithromycin **plus** a β-lactam such as IV co-amoxiclav.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman who had a stroke a month ago coughs during meals. She now has right lower lobe consolidation.
items.explanation: Post-stroke **dysphagia** means **aspiration**: Davidson gives **amoxicillin + metronidazole**.

items.stem: A man has been ventilated on ICU for 9 days and has had several antibiotic courses. He develops new infiltrates and purulent secretions; his unit has a high rate of MRSA.
items.explanation: **Late-onset HAP/VAP** needs antipseudomonal cover (**meropenem**) plus **MRSA** cover (**vancomycin** or linezolid).

items.stem: A 41-year-old man is in ICU with severe pneumonia; his urinary Legionella antigen is positive.
items.explanation: Severe **Legionella**: clarithromycin **plus IV rifampicin**.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is on day 5 of IV antibiotics for CAP. Her fever had settled but now swings to 39°C and her CRP is rising again. Chest X-ray shows a new moderate right pleural effusion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop antibiotics and repeat the X-ray in 6 weeks
questions.explanation: Persistent or recurrent fever with rising markers on appropriate antibiotics suggests **empyema**. Aspirate the effusion **under ultrasound** and send it for Gram stain, culture, protein, glucose, LDH and pH; an empyema needs **urgent drainage**.
whyNot: She is getting worse, so this is no time to step down.
Bronchoscopy looks for an obstructing lesion; the problem here is the new effusion.
Physiotherapy does not treat a pleural collection.
She has a probable empyema that needs diagnosis and drainage now.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with alcohol dependence vomited while heavily intoxicated two weeks ago. He now coughs up large amounts of foul-smelling sputum, has a high swinging fever and early finger clubbing. Chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity with an air–fluid level in the right lower lobe.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Aspiration while drunk, **foul sputum**, swinging fever, **rapid clubbing** and a **cavity with a fluid level** in the lung: a **lung abscess** from mixed oral anaerobes.
whyNot: Empyema is pus in the pleural space; the cavity here lies within the lung.
Bronchiectasis is chronic airway dilatation over years, not one new cavity with a fluid level after a single event.
TB cavitates too, but the aspiration history, foul sputum and short course favour an anaerobic abscess.
Mendelson’s syndrome is the acute chemical pneumonitis right after acid aspiration, not a cavity two weeks later.

questions.stem: A medical student asks why the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine gives longer-lasting protection than the polysaccharide vaccine.
questions.leadIn: What is the best explanation?
options: The protein carrier recruits T-cell help, generating immunological memory
It contains more serotypes than the polysaccharide vaccine
It is a live attenuated vaccine
It is given by a different route that boosts mucosal immunity
questions.explanation: Polysaccharide alone gives a weak T-cell response, so antibody is short-lived and there is **no memory**. Linking it to a **protein** (as in PCV and Hib vaccine) brings in **T-cell help** and memory.
whyNot: The opposite: the polysaccharide vaccine covers 23 serotypes and the conjugate 13 (Davidson).
Both pneumococcal vaccines are made from capsular polysaccharide; neither is live.
The route is not why memory develops; the protein conjugate is.
Both use purified capsular polysaccharide, not whole organisms.

questions.stem: An ICU team reviews its policy to reduce ventilator-associated and other hospital-acquired pneumonia.
questions.leadIn: Which measure is recommended?
options: Routine proton pump inhibitor for every patient
Prophylactic vancomycin for all ventilated patients
Nasogastric tubes for all elderly patients
questions.explanation: HAP mortality is around 30%, so prevention matters: hand hygiene, clean equipment, less aspiration, **fewer PPIs**, **2% chlorhexidine** mouth care, and sometimes selective digestive decontamination if ventilation will exceed 48 h.
whyNot: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis with PPIs should be **limited**, not given to everyone.
Blanket antibiotic prophylaxis is not a listed measure and drives resistance.
Nasogastric intubation **increases** aspiration risk.
Reduced consciousness and cough reflex **predispose** to HAP.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted with COVID-19 pneumonia confirmed by RT-PCR. He needs 4 L/min of oxygen to keep his saturation in range but is not ventilated.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment is indicated?
questions.explanation: Hospitalised COVID-19 needing **supplemental oxygen**: **dexamethasone ± remdesivir** (Pocket Medicine). Anticoagulation is also given because thrombosis is common.
whyNot: Oseltamivir treats influenza, not SARS-CoV-2.
Co-trimoxazole treats Pneumocystis pneumonia.
Molnupiravir is an option for high-risk patients **not** in hospital.
Amoxicillin treats bacterial CAP and does not act on the virus.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old engineer flew back from Saudi Arabia 5 days ago. He has fever, myalgia, dry cough and diarrhoea, and develops worsening hypoxia. Bloods show lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and a raised LDH.
questions.leadIn: Where should he be nursed while the diagnosis is confirmed?
options: Airborne infection isolation room with contact and airborne precautions
Open ward bay with standard precautions
Bay shared with other pneumonia patients
Side room with droplet precautions only, no respirator
questions.explanation: Travel to the Middle East plus severe pneumonia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised LDH suggests **MERS-CoV**. Davidson’s model: an **airborne infection isolation room** with **contact plus airborne** precautions and **PPE** for staff; confirm by PCR.
whyNot: MERS has spread person to person inside hospitals; standard precautions are not enough.
Cohorting an unconfirmed case with other patients risks spreading the infection.
Davidson specifies airborne as well as contact precautions.
He is hypoxic and deteriorating, so he needs hospital care.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man with pneumonia becomes anaemic during admission and his direct Coombs test is positive. Which test best supports the likely organism?
items.explanation: Haemolysis in a young adult with pneumonia suggests **Mycoplasma**; **cold agglutinins** are positive in about half of cases.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with oral candida and weight loss has a dry cough, desaturates when he walks, and has bilateral perihilar shadowing. Which test will confirm the cause of the pneumonia?
items.explanation: Probable **Pneumocystis** pneumonia (likely HIV). Confirm with **immunofluorescence on induced sputum or BAL**.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with COPD and CAP has SaO2 89% on air and is drowsy. What is the most urgent test before setting her oxygen?
items.explanation: **ABG** when SaO2 < 93% or the illness is severe, to look for **hypercapnia** and acidosis; COPD makes CO2 retention a real risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted with lobar pneumonia. He has no known risk factors. Which test should every adult with pneumonia be offered?
items.explanation: Kumar: offer an **HIV test** to all pneumonia patients.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 3-day history of fever and productive cough. You examine the right lower zone of her chest.
questions.leadIn: Which combination of signs indicates consolidation?
options: Dull percussion, bronchial breathing and whispering pectoriloquy
Stony dull percussion with absent breath sounds
Hyper-resonant percussion with absent breath sounds
Resonant percussion with widespread expiratory wheeze
Dull percussion with reduced breath sounds and the trachea pulled towards that side
questions.explanation: Consolidated lung conducts sound well: **dullness**, **bronchial breathing**, **whispering pectoriloquy** and crackles.
whyNot: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds is typical of a **pleural effusion**.
Hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds suggests a **pneumothorax**.
Resonance with wheeze suggests airway narrowing (asthma or COPD), not consolidation.
Tracheal pull towards the side suggests **lobar collapse**, e.g. from retained sputum.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has been on a surgical ward for 10 days after a laparotomy and received two antibiotic courses. He develops a new pneumonia.
questions.leadIn: Which organisms are most likely?
options: Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.explanation: **Late-onset HAP** (after 4–5 days) is mainly due to **Gram-negatives** (E. coli, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter), Staph. aureus including MRSA, and anaerobes.
whyNot: Mycoplasma is a community organism of young adults.
Psittacosis follows contact with birds.
Q fever follows exposure to farm animals.
A community-acquired atypical organism.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukaemia is neutropenic after chemotherapy. She has fever and a cough. HRCT shows a nodule surrounded by a rim of ground-glass attenuation.
questions.leadIn: Which infection does this sign suggest?
questions.explanation: A **halo sign** (intermediate attenuation around a nodule) in an immunocompromised host suggests **aspergillosis**.
whyNot: Pneumocystis gives diffuse bilateral (perihilar) shadowing, not a haloed nodule.
Pyogenic bacteria give focal consolidation, often with effusion.
Viruses tend to give bilateral opacities.
Legionella gives consolidation, not a haloed nodule.

questions.stem: Two adults are admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. You want the feature that favours Legionella over pneumococcus.
questions.leadIn: Which feature favours Legionella?
questions.explanation: **Legionella**: lymphopenia without marked leucocytosis, **hyponatraemia**, low albumin and raised transaminases. The other options all point to pneumococcus.
whyNot: Labial herpes suggests **pneumococcus**.
Rusty sputum suggests **pneumococcus**.
A marked neutrophilia fits **pneumococcus**.
Gram-positive diplococci are **Strep. pneumoniae**; Legionella is not seen on Gram stain.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with pneumonia is fully orientated. RR 30/min, BP 104/60 mmHg, urea 7.4 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is his CURB-65 score using the Davidson criteria?
questions.explanation: Score each item against Davidson’s cut-offs. **Step 1** Confusion: none = 0. **Step 2** Urea 7.4 > 7 = 1. **Step 3** RR must be **> 30**; 30 = 0. **Step 4** BP: systolic 104 is not < 90 and diastolic 60 is not **< 60** = 0. **Step 5** Age 66 > 65 = 1. Total **2**, so hospital-supervised treatment. With the NICE version in Zero to Finals (RR ≥ 30, diastolic ≤ 60) he would score 4; know which version your exam uses.
whyNot: Urea and age each score a point, so 1 is too low.
3 would need RR or BP to count, but neither crosses Davidson’s cut-off.
4 is the score with the NICE thresholds (≥ 30 and ≤ 60), not Davidson’s.
He is not confused, so 5 is impossible.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman with Parkinson’s disease and an unsafe swallow develops right lower lobe pneumonia after a choking episode at lunch. She had Clostridioides difficile colitis last year.
questions.leadIn: Which empirical regimen is most appropriate (Davidson)?
questions.explanation: **Step 1**: choking with an unsafe swallow = **aspiration pneumonia**. **Step 2**: the organisms are mixed oral **anaerobes and aerobes**, so anaerobic cover is needed. **Step 3**: Davidson’s choice is **amoxicillin + metronidazole**; co-amoxiclav has a suitable spectrum but **raises C. difficile risk**, which matters here. Kumar would use co-amoxiclav, but Davidson is the reference.
whyNot: The right spectrum, but Davidson warns of C. difficile risk, and she has already had it.
No reliable anaerobic cover.
Covers Staph. aureus only, not oral anaerobes.
Far too broad for community aspiration; keep it for late-onset HAP.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman on methotrexate and long-term prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis has a high fever, a dry cough and breathlessness. Her saturation falls sharply when she walks. Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar shadowing spreading outwards.
questions.leadIn: What is the first-line treatment for the most likely infection?
questions.explanation: **Step 1**: risk factors are **long-term steroids plus methotrexate**. **Step 2**: dry cough, **desaturation on exertion** and **perihilar butterfly** shadowing suggest **Pneumocystis jirovecii**. **Step 3**: confirm by immunofluorescence on induced sputum/BAL, and treat with **high-dose co-trimoxazole** (adding steroids only if HIV-positive).
whyNot: Amoxicillin does not cover Pneumocystis.
For Staph. aureus, not Pneumocystis.
For influenza; this picture is Pneumocystis.
An antipseudomonal agent; it does not treat Pneumocystis.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: On day 7 of treatment a 60-year-old man’s fever, which had settled, returns with a swinging pattern and his CRP rises. Pleural aspiration yields frank pus.
items.explanation: Pus in the pleural space is **empyema**; the clue is fever and markers rising again despite antibiotics. It needs urgent drainage.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman with pneumonia after abdominal surgery cannot cough because of pain. She suddenly becomes more breathless; the trachea has moved towards the affected side and the X-ray shows a dense opacity with volume loss.
items.explanation: Two steps: a weak cough from pain lets **sputum be retained**, and volume loss with tracheal shift towards the lesion means **lobar collapse**.

items.stem: A 28-year-old with post-influenza staphylococcal pneumonia develops sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness; one side is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
items.explanation: **Pneumothorax** is a recognised complication, especially with **Staph. aureus**.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man improving on day 4 of treatment for CAP develops palpitations; his pulse is irregularly irregular at 140/min.
items.explanation: **Arrhythmias**, especially **AF**, are listed complications of pneumonia.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old had a sore throat last week. He now has a painful, swollen neck, rigors and haemoptysis; CT shows internal jugular vein thrombosis and several cavitating lung nodules.
items.explanation: Sore throat → jugular thrombosis → septic lung abscesses = **Lemierre’s syndrome**, usually **Fusobacterium necrophorum**.

items.stem: A fit 24-year-old rugby player whose teammates have had recurrent boils develops a rapidly progressive necrotising pneumonia with haemoptysis.
items.explanation: Skin infections spreading through a team plus **necrotising pneumonia** suggest **PVL-producing CA-MRSA**.

items.stem: After 12 days of ventilation on ICU, a patient’s secretions grow a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism; the microbiologist advises a carbapenem, or colistin if it is resistant to that.
items.explanation: **Acinetobacter baumannii** is a classic MDR cause of VAP; usually carbapenem-sensitive, otherwise colistin.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with very poor dental hygiene has months of low-grade fever and weight loss from a chronic suppurative lung infection. The organism grows very slowly and needs 6–12 months of penicillin.
items.explanation: **Actinomycosis** (mostly A. israelii): chronic suppuration, poor teeth, slow growth, long penicillin course.

items.stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man has just returned from Riyadh with fever, myalgia, dry cough and diarrhoea. He has lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and a raised LDH, and is deteriorating towards respiratory failure.
items.explanation: Middle East travel with this laboratory pattern and rapid deterioration points to **MERS-CoV**; isolate and confirm by PCR.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP is improving on oral amoxicillin.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is an adequate total course length?
questions.explanation: Davidson: **5 days** suffices for most uncomplicated pneumonia; Legionella, staphylococcal and Klebsiella infections need longer.
whyNot: Shorter than any source recommends.
Closer to the Legionella course (14–21 days in K&C Essentials).
Again a Legionella-type duration, not routine CAP.
The sort of length used for some lung abscesses (4–6 weeks).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man returns from a conference at a large hotel and is diagnosed with Legionella pneumonia on urinary antigen testing.
questions.leadIn: Which additional step is most important for public health?
options: Notify the health authority so the source can be investigated
Nurse him in an airborne isolation room
Give prophylactic clarithromycin to his family
Screen his contacts with chest X-rays
questions.explanation: Legionella comes from **contaminated water systems**, so a case usually has to be **notified** so the source can be found and dealt with.
whyNot: Legionella is caught by inhaling aerosols from contaminated water, so the priority is the source, not isolating him.
Contacts do not catch it from him; prophylaxis is not indicated.
The sources offer no vaccine against Legionella; prevention means finding and treating the contaminated water source.
Screening contacts misses the point: the danger is the shared water source.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops pneumonia on day 3 after an elective knee replacement. She has had no antibiotics in recent months.
items.explanation: **Early-onset HAP** with no recent antibiotics: **co-amoxiclav or cefuroxime** (Davidson).

items.stem: A 63-year-old man develops pneumonia on day 3 of an admission for heart failure; he finished a course of antibiotics for a urinary infection last week.
items.explanation: Early HAP **after recent antibiotics**: **piperacillin–tazobactam** or a 3rd-generation cephalosporin.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man with CURB-65 0 pneumonia and no allergies is going home.
items.explanation: Uncomplicated CAP: **oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily**.

items.stem: A kidney transplant recipient on anti-rejection drugs has a high fever, dry cough, rapid desaturation on exertion and bilateral perihilar shadowing.
items.explanation: Two steps: transplant immunosuppression plus this picture = **Pneumocystis**, which is treated with **high-dose co-trimoxazole**.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with CAP is on the ward receiving IV antibiotics and high-concentration oxygen.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is an indication for ITU referral?
questions.explanation: Davidson Box 17.39: **persistent hypoxia (PaO2 < 8 kPa) despite high-concentration oxygen**, progressive hypercapnia, severe acidosis, shock, falling consciousness, or CURB-65 4–5 not responding quickly.
whyNot: A score of 2 means hospital-supervised care, not ITU.
Fever alone is not an ITU criterion.
Severity needs a WCC < 4 or > 20, and even that is not an ITU criterion on its own.
Treat with analgesia; it is not an ITU indication.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old abattoir worker develops a flu-like illness with high fever, headache and a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Q fever** (Coxiella burnetii) is linked with farm animals and **abattoir or hide workers**.
whyNot: Psittacosis follows contact with birds such as parrots.
Legionella comes from contaminated water systems in hotels and institutions.
Mycoplasma affects young people and has no occupational link.
Staph. aureus pneumonia follows influenza or staphylococcal septicaemia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman in hospital with COVID-19 pneumonia is already receiving dexamethasone. Over 12 hours her oxygen requirement climbs rapidly, but she is not yet intubated.
questions.leadIn: Which addition is recommended?
options: An anti-IL-6 agent such as tocilizumab
questions.explanation: Pocket Medicine: rapidly rising oxygen needs (or ventilation/ECMO) → **dexamethasone plus an anti-IL-6 agent (tocilizumab)** or a JAK inhibitor (baricitinib), with anticoagulation.
whyNot: Oseltamivir is for influenza.
Dexamethasone is the cornerstone for hypoxic inpatients; stopping it is wrong.
For Pneumocystis, not COVID-19.
Molnupiravir is for high-risk patients who are not in hospital.

ospe.identify: Sputum Gram stain: **Gram-positive diplococci** = **Streptococcus pneumoniae**, the commonest cause of CAP.
**Right middle lobe pneumonia**: opacity below the horizontal fissure with loss of the right heart border on the PA film; anterior consolidation on the lateral film.
**Lobar pneumonia**: dense, uniform consolidation confined to one lobe.
**Left lower zone lobar pneumonia**: ill-defined opacity with **no volume loss** (trachea and mediastinum central), as alveoli are filled with fluid.
**CURB-65 algorithm**: name the five criteria and the action for scores 0–1, 2 and ≥ 3.
